_comment: Mutants that survive for a reason somebody established, so that a run's
output can be read as 'what changed' rather than 'what is there'.
An entry is a claim that this specific change cannot be observed. Do not
add one on inspection alone: apply the mutation by hand, watch the suite
stay green, and say in `reason` what makes it unobservable. A mutant that
is merely untested is not equivalent -- it is a missing test.
And a green suite only proves equivalence over the inputs the fixtures
reach. A sibling repository nearly filed `make([]T, 0, len(a)+len(b))` with
`+` mutated to `-` as equivalent -- capacity is only a hint, the reasoning
is sound -- until `len(b) > len(a)` makes the capacity negative and panics.
Their fixture had both lengths at 1, so the suite stayed green and said
nothing. So the question is not whether the reasoning is right but over
which inputs it holds, and whether the fixtures go there.
Everything not listed here is reported as new. That is accurate rather
than noisy: the classifications made in earlier rounds live in tp closure
reasons, which is exactly the place a later round cannot read them from.
Moving one here is what makes it durable.

survivors.reason: baseOf takes the highest suffix an earlier round stored with `id.n > base`; `>=` assigns the value already held and changes nothing, which is the shape finding/id.go's NextID carries and says so in a comment. Verified by hand on 2026-09-18 -- applied `>=` through `go test -overlay`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/review` stayed green.

parseID refuses `n <= 0` after `strings.HasPrefix(rest, "0")` has already refused every spelling of zero, so `<` and `<=` differ only at n == 0, which cannot reach the comparison; a negative spelling (x-1) is refused by both. Verified by hand on 2026-09-18 -- applied `<` through `go test -overlay`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/proposal` stayed green.

anchorInsideUnit walks start+1..end after checking Contains(start) and Contains(end); `<=` adds only line end, already answered true two lines up, and when start >= end neither form iterates. Contains is a pure lookup. Verified by hand on 2026-09-13 -- applied `<=`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/cli` stayed green.

newRecordResult sizes honesty `2+len(found.unmappable)`; `2-len` would panic only past 2 entries, and resolveGapSupport, the only producer, appends to unmappable at most once (one GapUnmappable naming every unmapped probe), so the capacity is 2 or 1 and only a hint. Verified by hand on 2026-09-13 -- applied `-`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/cli` stayed green.

orphaned sizes a map `len(kept)+len(stored)`; `-` goes negative when the round already stores more records than the file keeps, but a map size hint below zero is treated as zero -- measured on go1.26.5, `make(map[string]bool, -4)` does not panic -- so contents and lookups are unchanged. Verified by hand on 2026-09-13 -- applied `-`, the full `./internal/cli` suite stayed green, and a direct orphaned call with 2 kept and 5 stored returned the right orphan.

NOT equivalent -- unobservable. `>= 0` makes settleStates resolve the role corpus and call MarkDuplicates on every run; MarkDuplicates over no orphans is a no-op, and the resolve reads the same two directories stampAxesAndClaims (record.go:451) resolved successfully earlier in the same run, so it can fail only if the corpus changes between the two lock-free reads. No seam injects that. Verified by hand on 2026-09-13 -- applied `>=`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/cli` stayed green.

waiversListResult.Text sizes its lines `2*len(r.Waivers)+1`; QUO makes it `2/len+1`. `len(r.Waivers) == 0` returns three lines above, so len >= 1 and the capacity is 3, 2 or 1 -- a hint append outgrows. Same shape as cli/context.go:48. Verified by hand on 2026-09-13 -- applied `/`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/cli` stayed green.

The `+1` on the same line as `-1`: past the early return len >= 1, so `2*len-1` >= 1, never the negative capacity make panics on. Verified by hand on 2026-09-13 -- applied `-`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/cli` stayed green.

NextID keeps the highest id seen, so `n > highest` and `n >= highest` assign the same value: on equality the assignment writes back what is already held. Verified by hand on 2026-09-01 -- applied `>=`, `go test ./internal/finding` stayed green. The comment above the line says the same thing, and it predates this file. Re-pointed from line 42 on 2026-09-13: f6402a0 added IDSuffix, twelve lines above NextID, and the one-package run of that day still reported the mutant LIVED at 54:48. Re-verified by hand the same day -- applied `>=` through `go test -overlay`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/finding` stayed green over the ids of earlier rounds and over ids cr did not write; applying `<=` instead failed TestAnIDCrDidNotWriteIsNotCounted, so the instrument was reaching the line.

rank cuts the qualified list with `qualified = qualified[:limit]`, and `>` against `>=` differs only when len(qualified) == limit, where the cut is `s = s[:len(s)]`: same length, same elements, and only the elements are copied out after it. limit is max(MaxCandidates, 0), so no negative bound reaches the slice. Verified by hand on 2026-09-11 -- applied `>=`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/reinvention` stayed green. The fixtures reach len < limit (4 against 5) and len > limit (4 against 3, 1 against 0 and -1) but not len == limit; that case is the identity reslice above, which the language fixes rather than a fixture.

Comment.String allocates `make([]string, 0, len(ownedRegions)+1)`, and `-1` changes only the capacity hint from 4 to 2: append grows the slice and the joined text is identical. The operand is not an input: ownedRegions is an unexported package var holding exactly the three owned regions of §8.1.3 and nothing appends to it, so the capacity is 2 on every call and never reaches the negative value that panics `make`. Verified by hand on 2026-09-11 -- applied `-1`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/render/` and `./internal/draft/` stayed green.

withoutRegion computes `length := strings.Index(text[start:], region.close)` where text[start:] begins with region.open, and `< 0` against `<= 0` differs only when length == 0, i.e. when the close marker matches at the very position the open marker starts. No input reaches that: each pair is `<!-- cr:NAME -->` against `<!-- cr:/NAME -->`, which differ at byte 8 ('/' against the name's first letter), inside both markers, so a string opening with one cannot open with the other. Verified by hand on 2026-09-11 -- applied `<= 0`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/render/` and `./internal/draft/` stayed green. The equivalence rests on that byte: a future region whose close marker is a prefix of its open marker would make the mutant observable.

NOT equivalent -- unobservable, and entered as such. The guard is `released := held.Unlock(); err == nil && released != nil`, and the mutant `err != nil` differs only when Unlock itself fails: then the original reports the release error after a good write and keeps the write error after a bad one, while the mutant does the reverse. gofrs/flock v0.13.0 returns an error from Unlock only when flock(LOCK_UN) fails on a descriptor it holds open and locked, and held is a local with no seam to inject that. Verified by hand on 2026-09-11 -- applied `err != nil`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/state` stayed green. Reaching it needs a seam in a closed task's production code for an error path the lock does not produce in practice; not worth that change. Revisit if the ledger's lock ever gains an injectable interface. Re-pointed from line 55 on 2026-09-13: 386cb5c moved the body into updateRepoStore, shared with triage.ndjson, and the guard and its column are unchanged there. Re-verified by hand the same day -- applied `err != nil` through `go test -overlay`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/state` stayed green; the lock is still a local `flock.New(lock)` and go.mod still pins gofrs/flock v0.13.0.

contextResult.Text sizes its line buffer `2*len(r.Notes)+1`, and MUL becoming QUO makes it `2/len(r.Notes)+1`. The one value that would divide by zero never reaches the line: `len(r.Notes) == 0` returns "no notes recorded against ..." three lines above. For every length of 1 or more the quotient is 2, 1 or 0, so the capacity stays positive, append grows the slice to whatever it needs, and the joined text is byte-identical. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 -- applied `/`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/cli` stayed green. The fixtures reach the zero case through the early return and lengths of 1 and more through the listing.

The `+1` on the same line, turned into `-1`: `2*len(r.Notes)-1`. Past the early return above, len is at least 1, so the capacity is at least 1 and never the negative value `make` panics on; beyond that it is only a hint. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 beside its neighbour -- applied `-`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/cli` stayed green.

words flushes a word on `word.Len() > 0`, and `>= 0` flushes at every separator too, appending empty strings to the result. words has exactly one caller, checkProtected, which asks two questions of each word: whether `carriers[word]` equals a protected token, and whether the word contains one. Neither is ever true of "" -- carriers has no empty key, and every protected token is a non-empty string that "" cannot contain -- so the deny-list verdict is identical for every name. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 -- applied `>= 0`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/config` stayed green over names with separators (post.gate_timeout_seconds, CR_HOME_LABEL), without them (postconfirm), and nested three deep (a.b.c). Re-pointed from line 179 on 2026-09-13: 81b058c added seven lines to the settings table above it and 594b281 added `force` to the protected tokens and three carriers, and the one-package run of that day reported the mutant LIVED at 190:17. The argument survives both additions -- every token, `force` included, is still non-empty and no carrier key is empty. Re-verified by hand the same day -- applied `>= 0` through `go test -overlay`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/config` stayed green over the same names plus the force-named ones (post.force_findings) and the new carriers (rules.enforce_min, stats.workforce).

reservedFields sizes its buffer `len(fields)+len(claimHashes)`, and `-` cannot drive that negative: both operands are package-level literals in this file, `fields` carries the whole of the section 6.1 table and `claimHashes` exactly two names, and nothing appends to either at runtime. The difference is a large positive number on every call, so the capacity stays a hint and the names returned are the same. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 -- applied `-`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/finding` stayed green. This is render/comment.go's case: the operand is not an input.

notAbove returns the computed grade when `settled >= standing`, and `>` changes only the tie. gradeStrength holds section 6.2's three grades once each, and rankIn answers with an index into it or with its length for a value it does not list. The clause before this one has already returned when standing is that length, so in the tie standing indexes a real element and `settled == standing` means both ranks index the same one -- which means computed and held are the same Grade, and returning either returns the same value. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 -- applied `>`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/finding` stayed green, and grade_test.go drives every ordered pair of the three grades, the equal ones included. A gradeStrength that listed a value twice would make it observable. Re-pointed from line 212 on 2026-09-13: 4f1c9c2 added twelve lines in one hunk near line 54, and notAbove itself is unchanged. Re-verified by hand the same day -- applied `>` through `go test -overlay`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/finding` stayed green, and dedup.go still holds gradeStrength as the three grades once each.

OpenStates sizes its buffer `len(states)-len(terminal)` and `+` only makes it larger, which append never notices. Both operands are package-level literals in this file, so no input reaches the arithmetic and the capacity cannot go negative in either direction. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 -- applied `+`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/finding` stayed green.

The same byte as the ARITHMETIC_BASE entry above, reported under a second mutator name: gremlins maps token.SUB to token.ADD for both, so the two records describe one edit. The single hand-applied `+` on 2026-09-12 verified both.

The id allocator keeps the highest number seen, so `n > highest` and `n >= highest` assign the same value: on equality the assignment writes back what is already held. It is finding/id.go:54's entry in another file, and the comment two lines above says as much. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 -- applied `>=`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/finding` stayed green.

The same allocator in note: `n > highest` against `n >= highest` assigns the value already held on equality. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 -- applied `>=`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/note` stayed green.

The same allocator in probe: `n > highest` against `n >= highest` assigns the value already held on equality. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 -- applied `>=`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/probe` stayed green.

The same allocator in run: `n > highest` against `n >= highest` assigns the value already held on equality. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 -- applied `>=`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/run` stayed green.

Tail.Write truncates what it is handed with `if len(p) > t.limit { p = p[len(p)-t.limit:] }`, and `>=` differs only at equality, where the reslice is `p[0:]`: same length, same bytes, same backing array. No negative limit reaches the index -- NewTail clamps with max(limit, 0), Tail's fields are unexported, and nothing in the tree builds one any other way. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 -- applied `>=`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/run` stayed green over writes below, at and above the limit.

The second half of the same function: `if len(t.held) > t.limit` trims what is retained, and `>=` differs only at equality, where `append(t.held[:0], t.held[0:]...)` copies the held bytes onto themselves. Same length, same bytes. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 beside its neighbour -- applied `>=`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/run` stayed green.

Enclosing keeps the innermost span by taking the one with the greatest start, and `found <= 0` would let the span at index 0 be replaced unconditionally. It cannot change the answer, because a file's spans are built in ascending start order and no two share one: Index.cover appends in the order rules.scan produced the declarations, scan walks the file's lines from the top, and match returns at most one declaration per line. So for every i past found, `spans[i].start > spans[found].start` already holds and the second clause is true whatever the first says. TestTheIndexIsOrderedByPathThenLine pins that order. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 -- applied `<=`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/symbol` stayed green over nested PHP classes and their methods, where two spans hold one line, as well as over Go declarations at file scope.

The tie-break on the same line, `spans[i].start > spans[found].start` against `>=`. Equality would need two spans of one file declared on the same line, which the scan cannot produce: match returns at most one declaration per line. The two comparisons therefore agree on every input, for the reason and on the evidence of the entry above. Verified by hand on 2026-09-12 -- applied `>=`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/symbol` stayed green.

refuseUnknownBlocks keeps the earliest block naming a record the round does not hold with `at < firstAt`, and `<=` differs only when two such blocks sit on the same line. None can: blocksOf is the only producer of the map and refuseUnknownBlocks' only source, it walks the draft one line at a time and adds at most one block per line with `at: i + 1`, and a second block for an id it already holds is refused with MalformedMarkerError before the map is returned. Every `at` in the map is therefore distinct, and the tie the mutant changes never arises. Verified by hand on 2026-09-13 -- applied `<=` through `go test -overlay`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/draft` stayed green over one unknown block and over two, the second case added the same day as TestTheEarliestUnknownBlockIsTheOneNamed and run 50 times under the mutant and green each time, since Go randomises the map order the two blocks are read in; the same test failed 50 of 50 under the `>=` negation on the same byte. A block producer that could place two blocks on one line would make it observable.

triageKey.raised is read by nothing: key() builds it, and mergeTriageEvents uses the whole struct only as a map key, where equality is the one thing asked of it. Negating `e.Action == ActionRaised` flips the bool for every event at once, so two events share a key under the mutant exactly when they share one under the original, and the merge overwrites and appends the same events at the same positions. Verified by hand on 2026-09-13 -- applied `!=` through `go test -overlay`, `go test -count=1 ./internal/finding` stayed green over a raise beside a retried outcome for one record in one round, a rewritten event, and keys differing in pull request, round and record. It would become observable the moment anything reads the field as a fact rather than as part of an identity, such as a key serialised or compared against an action.
